passages.t: ‘To the church of God in Corinth’: thanks for a troubled church
passages.happening:
Paul opens the letter the way letters of his day opened: the sender, the people he writes to, and a greeting.

The senders are “Paul, called to be an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and our brother Sosthenes” (verse 1). An apostle is someone sent with a message.

The church is named with care. It is “the church of God in Corinth” (verse 2). It belongs to God, not to Paul or to any leader. Its members are “sanctified in Christ Jesus and called to be holy” (verse 2). And they are not alone: they stand “together with all those everywhere who call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, their Lord and ours” (verse 2).

Then the greeting: “Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (verse 3).

Next comes a prayer of thanks. Paul thanks God for the grace given them. They have been made rich “in all speech and all knowledge” (verse 5). They do not lack any spiritual gift while they wait for Jesus to be revealed (verse 7). God will keep them strong to the end, so that they will be blameless on the day of the Lord (verse 8). The last word is about God, not about them: “God, who has called you into fellowship with His Son Jesus Christ our Lord, is faithful” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
A letter in the Greek world began with a short formula and a one-word greeting, ‘greetings’. Paul turns that word into grace, charis, God's free gift, and adds peace, the greeting of Jewish homes and the old Hebrew word shalom. So Jew and Gentile meet in the first lines.

‘Church’ is the Greek ekklēsia. In a Greek city it meant the assembly of citizens called together to do the city's business. The Greek translation of the Old Testament also used it for the assembly of Israel gathered before God. ‘The church of God in Corinth’ is God's own assembly, meeting in the middle of a Roman city.

‘Sanctified’ and ‘holy’ come from the same Greek root. To be holy is to be set apart for God. Paul calls these people holy before he corrects a single thing. Holiness is first something God has done, and only then something they must live out.

The first hearers would also notice what Paul thanks God for. Speech, knowledge and spiritual gifts were exactly what the Corinthians were proud of. Paul is glad of the gifts. But he thanks God for them, not the Corinthians. They are gifts, not achievements. Later he will ask, “What do you have that you did not receive?” (4:7).

And he points them forward. They are still waiting for the revelation of Jesus Christ, and the ‘day of our Lord’ is still to come. Some in Corinth seem to have thought they had already arrived. Paul's first prayer reminds them they have not.

‘Fellowship’ is the Greek koinōnia, a sharing, a partnership. They have been called into a shared life with God's Son. That is why their quarrels will matter so much.
passages.ot:
‘Those who call on the name of the Lord’ is the language of the Old Testament for people who worship the LORD. The prophet Joel promised, “And everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved” (Joel 2:32). Paul now speaks of people everywhere who call on the name of ‘our Lord Jesus Christ’. He uses for Jesus the words Israel used for its God.

‘The day of our Lord Jesus Christ’ (verse 8) takes up the prophets' ‘day of the LORD’, the day God would come to judge and to put things right. Amos warned, “Woe to you who long for the Day of the LORD!” (Amos 5:18). Paul now speaks of that day as the day of Jesus.

‘God is faithful’ (verse 9) echoes the song of Moses: “A God of faithfulness without injustice, righteous and upright is He” (Deuteronomy 32:4).
passages.asks: Paul thanks God for a church that was deeply troubled, before he says a word of correction. Ask whether you can thank God honestly for people you are disappointed in. Ask, too, what gifts you have been given that you are tempted to treat as your own work. And notice where Paul ends: not with the Corinthians' strength, but with God's faithfulness. Ask what it would mean to rest on that rather than on yourself.

passages.t: ‘I follow Paul’, ‘I follow Apollos’: a divided church
passages.happening:
Paul turns at once to the problem. “I appeal to you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that all of you agree together, so that there may be no divisions among you” (verse 10).

He has heard the news from Chloe's household: there are quarrels (verse 11). He spells it out. “Individuals among you are saying, ‘I follow Paul,’ ‘I follow Apollos,’ ‘I follow Cephas,’ or ‘I follow Christ.’” (verse 12).

Then three sharp questions. “Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Were you baptized into the name of Paul?” (verse 13).

Paul says he is glad he baptized only a few of them: Crispus and Gaius, and the household of Stephanas. He cannot remember any others (verses 14-16). No one can say they were baptized into his name.

“For Christ did not send me to baptize, but to preach the gospel, not with words of wisdom, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power” (verse 17). That last phrase opens the long argument that follows.
passages.hearers:
Apollos was a learned Jew from Alexandria in Egypt, a gifted speaker who knew the Scriptures well. He had taught in Corinth after Paul left (Acts 18:24-28). Cephas is the Aramaic form of the name Peter; both mean ‘rock’. Whether Peter himself had visited Corinth is not known. Some members may simply have claimed his authority.

There is no sign that Paul, Apollos and Peter were rivals. Later in the letter Paul says he strongly urged Apollos to visit Corinth again (16:12). The rivalry was among the Corinthians.

Greek and Roman cities loved public speakers. Teachers of rhetoric, the art of persuasive speech, gathered students and fans, and people attached themselves to favourite speakers. Being the follower of an impressive teacher raised your own standing. The Corinthians seem to have treated Christian leaders the same way. Apollos, eloquent and learned, may have seemed more impressive than Paul.

What about ‘I follow Christ’? Readers differ. Some think it was a fourth party who claimed to be above the others. Others think Paul adds it with irony, to show how absurd the slogans are: Christ is not one leader among several.

Chloe was probably a woman of some means, and ‘Chloe's household’ were probably her slaves or workers travelling on business between Corinth and Ephesus. Crispus had been the leader of the synagogue in Corinth before he believed (Acts 18:8). Gaius may be the same Gaius who later hosted the whole church (Romans 16:23).

Notice Paul's honesty about his memory in verse 16. He is dictating, and he corrects himself as he goes. This is a real letter, spoken aloud.
passages.ot:
Paul's appeal for unity draws on what Israel was always meant to be: one people under one God. A psalm sings, “Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers live together in harmony” (Psalm 133:1).

The questions in verse 13 stand on the teaching of Jesus himself, who prayed for those who would believe in him “that all of them may be one” (John 17:21).

Baptism ‘into the name’ of someone meant being handed over to that person, to belong to them. Jesus sent his followers to baptize “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). No one in Corinth had been baptized into Paul. That is his whole point.
passages.hard:
“For Christ did not send me to baptize” (verse 17). Does this mean baptism does not matter?

No. Paul did baptize people, as he has just said. He treats baptism as a deep and shared thing later in this same letter: “For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body” (12:13). In Romans he speaks of being “baptized into His death” (Romans 6:3). What Paul means here is that his own calling was to preach. Others could baptize the people who came to faith. And he is glad of it, because in Corinth people were boasting about who had baptized them, as if baptism tied you to a leader.

Christians hold different views about baptism: who should be baptized, how, and what it does. The note on Acts 2:37-41 sets out the main views fairly. All agree with Paul here: baptism joins a person to Christ, not to the person who does the baptizing.

The other half of the verse matters just as much. Paul would not preach ‘with words of wisdom’. He does not mean he spoke carelessly or without thought; his letters are full of careful argument. He means he would not use the tricks of the clever speaker to win admirers. If people were won by his skill, the cross would be ‘emptied of its power’.
passages.asks: Ask whose name you are tempted to put before Christ's: a preacher, a writer, a movement, a church, a tradition. There is nothing wrong with learning from a teacher. It goes wrong when a teacher becomes a badge that sets you above others. Paul's questions are still the test. Was this person crucified for you? Into whose name were you baptized?

passages.t: The message of the cross: foolishness and power
passages.happening:
“For the message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God” (verse 18).

Paul quotes the prophet Isaiah: God will destroy the wisdom of the wise (verse 19). Then he asks where the wise man is, and the scribe, and the debater of this age. “Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world?” (verse 20).

The world, with all its wisdom, did not come to know God. So God chose to save those who believe through what looked like a foolish message (verse 21).

“Jews demand signs and Greeks search for wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles” (verses 22-23). But to those God calls, Jews and Greeks alike, Christ is “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (verse 24).

Paul ends with a riddle: “For the foolishness of God is wiser than man’s wisdom, and the weakness of God is stronger than man’s strength” (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
To hear this passage as the first hearers did, you have to feel how shameful the cross was. Crucifixion was the death Rome kept for slaves, bandits and rebels, a slow and public death meant to shame. The Roman orator Cicero once said in court that the very word cross should be kept far from a Roman citizen's thoughts, eyes and ears. Polite people did not talk about it.

Now imagine a message whose centre is a crucified man, named as Lord and as God's wisdom. To an educated Greek it sounded absurd. To a Jew it sounded worse. The law said, “anyone who is hung on a tree is under God’s curse” (Deuteronomy 21:23). How could the Messiah, God's chosen king, die under a curse?

‘Stumbling block’ is the Greek skandalon, a trap or something that trips you. ‘Foolishness’ is mōria, from which English gets the word moron.

Paul is not mocking the questions people asked. He describes two ways of asking for proof. Some asked for signs: let God show his power in a great act, as he did at the Red Sea. Others asked for wisdom: let the message make sense by the best thinking of the day. Both are natural things to want. Paul says God answered both in a way no one expected: power shown in weakness, wisdom shown in a cross.

The word ‘Greeks’ here, and ‘Gentiles’ in verse 23, stands for the non-Jewish world as a whole. The church in Corinth was made of both.
passages.ot:
Paul quotes Isaiah 29:14. In the Hebrew, from which the Berean Standard Bible translates Isaiah, God says, “The wisdom of the wise will vanish, and the intelligence of the intelligent will be hidden” (Isaiah 29:14). Paul's wording, “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise” (verse 19), is close to the old Greek translation. Either way the setting is the same. Isaiah spoke to the leaders of Jerusalem, who trusted their own clever plans and honoured God with their lips while their hearts were far from him (Isaiah 29:13). God would overturn their cleverness. Paul sees God doing it again.

‘Where is the wise man?’ (verse 20) echoes questions in Isaiah too, where the prophet mocks the advisers of proud kings (Isaiah 19:12; 33:18).

Behind the stumbling block is a stone. Isaiah speaks of God laying “a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation” in Zion (Isaiah 28:16), and of a stone that would make people stumble (Isaiah 8:14). The first Christians read both of Jesus.
passages.hard:
Does ‘Jews demand signs and Greeks search for wisdom’ insult Jews or Greeks?

No. Paul is describing two ways of asking God for proof, not passing judgment on two peoples. He was a Jew himself, and he spoke Greek and knew Greek thought. In the very next verse he says that God calls ‘both Jews and Greeks’ (verse 24). The church he writes to was made of both. No one in the room is left outside, and no one is above anyone else.

Any reading that turns these words into contempt for Jewish people, as if they were simply blind, is false, and these notes reject it. Paul says the same message is foolishness to the clever Greek. His point is that the cross humbles everyone's way of reaching God, the religious person's and the thinker's alike.

Is Paul against thinking, then? No. He argues carefully all through this letter, and he calls Christ ‘the wisdom of God’. What he rejects is the claim that human cleverness can find its own way to God, and the habit of ranking people by how clever or impressive they are. Christians have long held that reason is God's gift and serves faith well, but that the gospel cannot be worked out by reason alone.
passages.asks: Ask what kind of proof you have wanted from God: a sign, or an argument that leaves no room for trust. Both are understandable. Then ask what it would mean to look for God where Paul says he is found, in a crucified man. And ask whether there is anything in the message of the cross that still embarrasses you, and why.

passages.t: ‘Not many of you were wise’: God chose the lowly
passages.happening:
Paul tells the Corinthians to look at themselves. “Brothers, consider the time of your calling: Not many of you were wise by human standards; not many were powerful; not many were of noble birth” (verse 26).

“But God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise; God chose the weak things of the world to shame the strong” (verse 27). He chose the lowly and despised, even the things that are not, to bring to nothing the things that are (verse 28). The purpose: “so that no one may boast in His presence” (verse 29).

Everything they have comes from God. “It is because of Him that you are in Christ Jesus, who has become for us wisdom from God: our righteousness, holiness, and redemption” (verse 30).

So, as Scripture says, “Let him who boasts boast in the Lord” (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
Corinth was a city where people worked hard to be someone. Wealthy citizens paid for buildings and had their names cut in stone. Freed slaves rose to riches and office. Birth, wealth, education and connections decided who counted.

Paul's three words line up with that world. ‘Wise’ means educated. ‘Powerful’ means people of influence. ‘Of noble birth’ means people from good families. Not many in the church were any of these.

Notice the words ‘not many’. That means some were. The church held a few people of means, such as Gaius, who later hosted the whole church (Romans 16:23), and Crispus, who had led the synagogue (Acts 18:8). But most were ordinary: workers, the poor, slaves and freed slaves. The quarrels in this letter often run along the line between the few and the many.

‘Boast’ was not only a private feeling. In Corinth people advertised their achievements and connections in public. Paul says that before God no one can do that.

Verse 30 gathers the whole of salvation into Christ. ‘Righteousness’ is being set right with God. ‘Holiness’ is being set apart for him. ‘Redemption’ is a word from the slave market and the law of Israel: being bought back, set free at a price.
passages.ot:
Paul's closing words come from Jeremiah. The whole passage reads: “Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, nor the strong man in his strength, nor the wealthy man in his riches” (Jeremiah 9:23). Then: “But let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows Me, that I am the LORD” (Jeremiah 9:24). The wise, the strong and the rich in Jeremiah match Paul's wise, powerful and well-born in verse 26 almost exactly. Paul has been following Jeremiah all along.

God's choice of the lowly runs through the Old Testament. Hannah sang, “He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap” (1 Samuel 2:8). God told Israel he did not choose them because they were many: “you were the fewest of all peoples” (Deuteronomy 7:7).
passages.asks: Paul tells the Corinthians to remember who they were when God called them. Ask what you were, and had, when God first found you. Ask whether you now measure other believers by education, money, family or influence. And ask what you are tempted to boast in. Jeremiah's answer is still the one Paul gives: boast that you know the Lord.
